opening_summary: Thirty-two terms for finding your way around the Unity editor, from its windows to Play Mode, prefabs, tags, layers and settings. The main parts are matched to their Godot equivalents.
opening_description: 32 Unity editor terms: windows, prefabs, settings.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers to Unity often think the Scene view is what the player sees. It is not. The Scene view is a free editor camera you steer while you build. The Game view is what the game's camera shows. Unity is full of look-alike pairs like that. This film goes through its terms, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
The Scene view is
what the player sees.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-two terms for finding your way around the Unity editor, in four groups. The first group is windows and the toolbar. The Scene view, Game view, Hierarchy, Project window, Inspector, Console, Toolbar, and Layout and tabs. Where each thing sits, and what it is for.

The second group is objects and moving around. GameObject, Component, local and world space, pivot handles, the Scene gizmo, orbit, pan and zoom, Flythrough and the transform tools. What you select, and how you look at it and move it.

The third group is Play, prefabs, tags and layers. Play Mode, the changes Play Mode loses, Enter Play Mode Options, Prefab, Prefab Mode, the Overrides dropdown, Tag and Layer. What survives Play, and how objects are grouped.

The fourth group is assets, settings and measuring. Import settings, the Package Manager, Project Settings, Preferences, Build Profiles, the Animation window, the Animator window and the Profiler. Where options are kept, and how you check speed.

This is a drawing of the Unity editor, with the Scene view lit in red in the middle. The Scene view is where you look at the scene and edit it, through a free editor camera that you steer yourself. Here the Move handle drags the Player from x equals zero to x equals four. For example, to put a coin above a gap in your platformer, you drag it into place in the Scene view.

The Game view sits on the tab beside it. It shows what the scene's cameras render, as a player would see it. Here it draws two of the four objects, the two inside the camera's frame. For example, after placing that coin, you switch to the Game view to check that the player's camera really shows it when the level starts.

The Hierarchy, on the left, is a tree of every GameObject in the open scene. Dragging one object onto another nests it as a child. Here the Mob row is selected, and the Inspector switches to show the Mob and its MobMove script. For example, you drag a sword onto the Player in the Hierarchy, so the sword becomes the player's child and travels with it.

The Project window, at the bottom, is a file browser for the project's Assets and Packages folders. It shows files on disk, not objects in the scene. Here the player picture is selected, and the Inspector shows its import settings, a Max Size of two thousand forty-eight with mipmaps off. For example, a new enemy sprite that you add to the Art folder turns up in the Project window, ready to drag into a level.

The same editor drawing, now with the Inspector lit on the right. The Inspector shows the components and settings of the selected object and lets you edit them. Here the Player's Speed goes from five to seven point five. The Hierarchy says which objects exist, and the Inspector says how the selected one is set. For example, select a moving platform and raise the speed its script shows in the Inspector, without opening any code.

The Console shares the bottom panel with the Project window. It lists messages, warnings and errors from your scripts and from the editor. Here there is one of each. Player ready, Mob has no collider, and a null reference error on line twelve of the player script. For example, if your coin script tries to use a score object that was never assigned, the Console shows that error and the line it came from.

The Toolbar is the strip across the top. It holds the transform tools, the pivot and handle toggles, and the Play, Pause and Step buttons. Here Play runs ninety frames, Pause holds the game, and three presses of Step add three more, so it stops at frame ninety-three. For example, to see the exact frame where a jump lands, you pause and step forward one frame at a time.

Layout and tabs is how you arrange the windows. Drag a tab to dock its window somewhere else, or pick a saved arrangement from the Layout menu at the top right. This menu lists Default, two by three, Tall and Wide. For example, while you tune an enemy's patrol, you can drag the Game tab beside the Scene view and watch both at once.

A drawing of one world from above, with eight objects and a camera's cone. The Scene view is the editor's view of that world, through a free camera you steer. It shows you all eight objects, plus the shape of the game camera's cone, with four inside it. For example, in the Scene view you can see a secret coin tucked off to the side, even where the player's camera never looks.

The Game view shows only what the game's camera renders. As the camera sweeps, the strip below draws just the objects inside the cone, so its count changes as the camera turns. At the end it shows four of eight. For example, a coin placed outside the camera's view is plain to see in the Scene view, but missing from the Game view, so the player never sees it.

A Hierarchy tree beside an Inspector for the Player. A GameObject is Unity's object, the thing each row of the Hierarchy stands for. On its own it does nothing until components are added. Here the Player starts with one component, the Transform, which holds its position, rotation and scale. For example, an empty GameObject named Coin sits in the level, invisible and inert, until you give it parts.

A Component is one piece of behaviour or data attached to a GameObject, and each one adds one job. Here a Sprite Renderer draws the picture, a Rigidbody 2D adds gravity and contact, and a PlayerMove script moves it. Four components, four jobs. For example, to finish that coin, you add a Sprite Renderer to draw it, a collider so it can be touched, and your own coin script to count it.

Local and world space are two ways to give a position. Local is relative to the parent object, and world is relative to the whole level. The Sword is a child of the Player, one unit to its right. When the Player moves from four to eight, the Sword's world x goes from five to nine, while its local x stays one. For example, a hat on your character keeps the same local position as the character runs across the level.

Pivot and Local handles are two toolbar toggles. Pivot or Center sets where the handle sits, at the object's pivot or the center of its bounds. Here the bounds run from minus forty to one hundred sixty, so Center puts the handle at sixty. Local or Global sets which way it points. Local turns with the object to thirty degrees, Global stays at zero. For example, to move a tilted ramp along its own slope, switch to Local, so the arrows tilt with it.

A wireframe cube, seen through the Scene view's editor camera. The Scene gizmo is the small axis widget at the Scene view's top right. Pick one of its axis cones and the view snaps to look straight along that axis. Here it steps through Top, Front and Right. For example, to check that the platforms in a side-on level line up, you pick the Front view and compare their heights directly.

Orbit, pan, zoom are three ways to move the editor camera around what you are looking at. Orbit turns around a point, pan shifts the view sideways, and zoom changes the distance, here to five point five. In the editor, Alt with a left drag orbits, a middle drag pans, and the scroll wheel zooms. For example, you orbit around a new enemy model to check its back, then zoom in on its feet.

Flythrough moves the camera itself, as if you were walking through the level. Hold the right mouse button and press W, A, S, D. Here W is held for two seconds at three units a second, and the camera flies forward past three cubes. Orbit turns around a point, and Flythrough moves the camera. For example, you fly down a long corridor level to check every doorway, without moving any object.

The Transform tools are the handles for changing a selection, Move, Rotate, Scale, Rect and Hand. Here the selected cube is moved, then rotated, then scaled up to one point five. Move, Rotate and Scale change the object itself, while orbit and Flythrough only change your view of it. For example, you use Scale to make one crate in a level bigger, and Rotate to tilt a platform into a ramp.

A timeline of ten seconds, made up for this example. Play Mode is when the editor runs the game inside itself. The Play button turns it on and off, and the editor is tinted while you are in it. Here Play starts at two seconds and stops at eight. The rest is Edit Mode, where changes are kept. For example, you press Play to try a new jump right inside the editor, without building the game.

Play Mode changes lost means edits to scene objects made during Play Mode are thrown away when you stop. In this made-up run, the Player's Speed is edited from five to nine at four seconds, and on exit it goes back to five. For example, you tune an enemy's patrol speed while playing, it finally feels right, and then you press stop and the old number is back.

The dashed line is a different kind of value, a run speed kept in a ScriptableObject, a data asset that belongs to the project, not to the scene. Edited to nine in Play Mode, it stays nine after exit. Only scene objects are reset. To keep a scene edit, copy the component's values before you exit. For example, a jump height stored in a tuning asset keeps the value you set while playing.

Enter Play Mode Options is a Project Settings choice to skip reloading the code, the scene, or both, when Play starts, so it starts faster. These times are invented. Reloading both takes six seconds, the default reloads only the scene in three, and not reloading at all takes half a second. The catch is that static values and old objects can carry over. For example, a static coin counter could start a new run still holding the last run's total.

A coin prefab asset, above five copies of it in a scene. A Prefab is Unity's reusable object template, and edits to it flow to every instance, every copy placed in a scene. The asset holds Value one. Three copies show it, and two carry an override, a value changed on that copy alone, of five and seven. For example, you build one coin with its sprite, collider and script, save it as a prefab, and drop copies all over a level.

Prefab Mode opens a prefab asset on its own, so you edit the template and not one instance. The header reads Scene, then Coin. Here the coin's Value is changed to two. Three instances follow it, and the two with overrides keep their own values. For example, to give every coin in your game a new pickup sound, you open the coin in Prefab Mode and change it once.

The Overrides dropdown lists an instance's changes. Apply pushes a change into the prefab, and Revert drops it. Here Apply pushes instance two's value of five into the prefab, so the template becomes five. Then Revert on instance four throws away its seven, and all five copies match. For example, you resize one coin in a level, like the result, and Apply it, so every coin gets the new size.

A table of twelve objects, each with a tag and a layer. A Tag is a text label on an object, for finding and filtering it by name. Here a search for the Enemy tag finds four of the twelve. A tag is a text label for lookup, and a layer is a number for rendering and physics. For example, your game over script can find every object tagged Enemy and freeze them all when the player dies.

A Layer is a numbered category, one per object, used to filter rendering or collisions. You set it in the Layer dropdown at the top of the Inspector. Here the Enemies layer is hidden in the Scene view, so three objects fade and nine remain. The Game view still draws them. For example, you put every enemy on an Enemies layer, so the player's sword can be set to collide with that layer only.

Tag and layer are set separately. The Ghost carries the Enemy tag, but sits on the Default layer. So the tag finds four enemies, while hiding the Enemies layer hides only three, and the Ghost stays visible. For example, if a new enemy has the right tag but the wrong layer, your enemy-finding code sees it, yet the player's sword passes straight through it.

Three bars of memory for one texture, two thousand forty-eight pixels square. Asset import settings are the options for how one asset is imported, such as a texture's Max Size and compression. They show in the Inspector and are saved in the asset's meta file, beside it. Compressed at full size it takes five point six megabytes, and at Max Size one thousand twenty-four, one point four. For example, a background picture that never fills the screen can take a smaller Max Size.

The Package Manager is the window, under the Window menu, that adds, updates and removes packages. A package is code or assets added to a project, unlike import settings, which change how one asset is imported. Installing one adds a line to the manifest file in the Packages folder. Here the dependencies go from two to three. For example, when your platformer needs the Input System package for its jump action, you install it here, and it appears as a new line in the manifest.

Four made-up teammates and one shared project. Project Settings belong to the project and are saved in it, such as Tags and Layers, Physics and Time. Here one person adds a layer, it is saved in the project folder, and after the others pull the commit, it reaches all four of them. For example, the gravity in your platformer's Physics settings belongs to the project, so every teammate's player falls the same way.

Preferences belong to you and your machine, such as colours, key shortcuts and which script editor opens. They are not in the repository. Here Ben switches his theme to Light, and the change reaches only him, one of four. Project Settings belong to the project, and Preferences belong to you. For example, choosing which code editor opens your player script is a Preference, and nobody else on the team gets it.

Build Profiles, under the File menu, are saved sets of build settings, one for each platform, with the target and the scenes to include. Each profile is an asset file, so it can be committed. Here there are three profiles, and the WebGL one includes three of the four scenes, leaving out Test. For example, a WebGL profile for posting your game on the web would include the boot scene and the levels, but not a test scene.

A jump clip on a timeline, with a square that rises and falls. The Animation window is where you key properties over time to make an Animation Clip. Here three keys, at zero, half a second and one second, set the height, and Unity fills in the frames between. Adding the first clip to an object also adds an Animator. For example, you key a coin's height at three moments to make it bob up and down.

The Animator window is where an Animator Controller's states and transitions are drawn and tested. The Animation window makes a clip, and the Animator window chooses which clip plays. In this simulated run, Speed passes zero point one and the state moves from Idle to Run, then a Jump trigger moves it to Jump. For example, your player's idle, run and jump clips sit here as states, joined by arrows that fire on its speed or on a jump trigger.

The Profiler measures how long each frame takes, split by system, such as scripts, rendering and physics, so you can find what is slow. In this simulated run of forty frames, three go over the budget of sixteen point seven milliseconds, sixty frames per second. The worst, frame twelve, takes thirty-three point four, and scripts are its largest share, fifteen. For example, if your game stutters whenever many coins spawn, the Profiler shows whether the time goes to scripts or to rendering.
This table matches parts of the Unity editor to their Godot equivalents, one row at a time. The Scene view, where you edit the world, matches the 2D or 3D main screen in Godot.
The Game view shows what the player sees, the picture from the game's own camera. In Godot, that is the running game window.
The Hierarchy, the tree of objects in the open scene, matches the Scene dock in Godot. Both list what the scene holds, with children nested under their parents.
The Project window, which shows the files in the project, matches the FileSystem dock in Godot. Both show files on disk, not objects in the scene.
The Inspector, for an object's properties and components, keeps its name in Godot. Godot's Inspector shows a node's properties, and its signals sit in a separate Node dock.
The Console, where messages, warnings and errors appear, matches two panels in Godot, the Output panel and the Debugger panel.
Play, Pause and Step run the game inside the Unity editor. In Godot, the matching controls are the Run, Pause and Stop buttons.
A Prefab, Unity's reusable object template, matches a saved scene in Godot that is instanced. A coin saved as its own scene and placed many times plays the part of a prefab.
Build Profiles, one build setup per platform, match the Export dialog in Godot and its export presets file, which is saved in the project the same way.
The Animator window, a state graph of clips, matches the AnimationTree in Godot. Both decide which animation clip plays, and when it changes.
The Profiler, which shows time per system per frame, matches the Profiler and Monitors in Godot's Debugger. Both are where you measure speed instead of guessing.
Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. The Scene view is the editor camera you steer, and here it orbits. The Game view is what the game's camera renders, and its frame stays fixed.
A Prefab asset is the template file, which you edit once. A Prefab instance is one copy in a scene, which may override. Here the asset holds Value two, and instance two keeps its own five.
A Tag is a text label, any name you create, for finding objects by name. A Layer is one of thirty-two numbers, for filtering. Here it is layer eight, of zero to thirty-one.
Project Settings are saved in the project and shared, so all three people here get the change. Preferences are saved on your machine and are yours alone. Only Ben changed his.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction, beside a chart of what it does. Show less of the world becomes, set the Main Camera's Field of View from sixty to forty. At ten units away, the visible height drops from eleven point five to seven point three.
Keep my Play Mode tweak becomes, Copy Component in Play Mode, exit, then Paste Component Values. Without the copy, Speed is back to five after exit. With the paste, it stays nine.
Update all the coins becomes, open Prefab Mode on Coin and set Value to two, and instances with an override keep theirs. Three of five change to two, and two keep their override.
Hide the enemies while I edit becomes, turn off the Enemies layer in the Layers dropdown, for the Scene view only. Nine of twelve stay visible, and three are hidden.

Make the texture smaller becomes, in its Inspector set Max Size from two thousand forty-eight to one thousand twenty-four and press Apply. Uncompressed, that is twenty-two point four megabytes down to five point six, a quarter of the memory.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you change something in the Unity editor. First, am I in the Scene view, where I edit, or the Game view, which shows what the player sees?
Second, is the editor tinted? Then I am in Play Mode, and any edit I make to scene objects will be thrown away when I stop.
Third, am I editing a prefab instance, one copy in the scene, or the prefab asset, the template that every copy follows?
Fourth, do I need a tag, to find objects by name, or a layer, to filter them by number for rendering or collisions?
Fifth, is this setting for the whole project, for me alone as a Preference, or for one build, in a Build Profile?
Sixth, does the Console show errors, and is the Profiler number measured, not guessed? Then say it exactly. Not fix the prefab, but Apply the Value override on instance two.

recap_lines: The Scene view is your editor camera, and the Game view is what players see.
A GameObject does nothing until you add components to it.
Scene edits made in Play Mode are thrown away when you stop.
Edit the prefab asset, and every instance without an override follows.
A tag finds objects by name, and a layer filters them by number.
Project Settings are shared with the team, and Preferences stay on your machine.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on the Unity editor with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms Scene view, Game view, Hierarchy, Inspector, Play Mode, Prefab, Overrides dropdown, Tag, Layer and Project Settings. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a small Unity task, and the answer waits for your reply.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 8 (Prefab, Prefab Mode and the Overrides dropdown) step 1: the caption says 'One asset, five copies, each showing Value 1.' but the picture shows instances #2 and #4 with overrides of Value 5 and Value 7, and the counter below says 'Instances showing the prefab's value: 3 of 5'. The narration follows the picture.

Slide 6 step 3: the label 'W held 2.0 s at 3 units/s: z = 2.0' reads as if 2 s at 3 units/s moved the camera 2 units. In renderNav the camera starts at z = 8 (z = 8 - 3*2*t), so 2.0 is the end position after 6 units of travel; the start position is never shown. The narration gives the time and speed only.
Slide 6 step 4: the label under the Scene gizmo, which shows the view name in steps 1 to 3 (Right, Persp), switches to the tool name (Move, Rotate, Scale), so the gizmo appears to say 'Scale'.
Slide 1 says '32 terms ... Each one is matched to its Godot part on the last term slide.' Slide 13 maps 11 rows, not 32 terms.
Slide 4 step 2: the GAME VIEW strip is drawn over the 'TELL THESE APART' heading, which is half hidden.

Slide 3 step 2: the Console error is 'NullReference: Player.cs:12', but the Project window lists only Move.cs and the Player's script component is PlayerMove; no Player.cs exists in the drawing. The Inspector's Speed also shows 5.0 again after step 1 set it to 7.5.
Slide 14 pair 4 shows three people ('all 3 get the change') where slide 11 uses a team of four.

Term names differ between the map and the term slides: the map says 'Import settings', 'changes lost', 'pivot handles' and 'orbit pan zoom', the slides say 'Asset import settings', 'Play Mode changes lost', 'Pivot and Local handles' and 'Orbit, pan, zoom'.

Slide 8 cites the glossary for 'Overrides dropdown' with the tag 'in the glossary', but the glossary has Override, Apply, Revert, Prefab asset and Prefab instance rows and no 'Overrides dropdown' row. Likewise slide 1's note says 32 terms while 'Edit Mode', 'Prefab asset' and 'Prefab instance' appear only in TELL THESE APART boxes.
